title: The Endurance of François K
summary: A conversation about late-1970s New York, the dancefloor as a space for community and François Kevorkian’s contemporary work reconstructing classic recordings live.
transcript:
François Kevorkian, known as François K, spoke with Breaking and Entering over Zoom ahead of his set at Golden Plains. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 26 February 2026. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: 'Go Bang', in the François K mix, is the definitive dancefloor anthem. Legend has it that Arthur Russell brought François K in in 1982 to fix the original album version, which DJs apparently found too complex, and François Kevorkian famously mixed it on borrowed time at Right Track Studios to create the version we know.

To give a little context to anyone arriving more recently to his music: he arrived in New York City in September 1975 with no money, apparently, and nowhere to stay. He trained as a jazz drummer in France under Tony Williams, who was Miles Davis's drummer, and decided at the age of 21 that New York was where he needed to be.

Within two years he was holding the Saturday-night residency at New York New York, one of the city's premier clubs, and within three years he was at Prelude Records, where his remix of Musique's 'In the Bush' became a huge hit. Through the early 80s he held the record for the most number-one 12-inch singles on Billboard's dance music chart: records by Yazoo, D-Train, Sharon Redd and Dinosaur L.

He's one of the only DJs ever invited to play at Paradise Garage, The Loft and Better Days, the three spaces that really defined New York's underground in that era, and he was a very close friend and collaborator of Larry Levan, another pioneering figure. Others might know François K because he mixed Depeche Mode's Violator in 1990, a record that sold somewhere between seven and 25 million copies, depending on which charts you look at.

He had a studio in the same building as Studio 54, founded parties that continue to this day with his friends Danny Krivit and Joe Claussell, worked with Haruomi Hosono of Yellow Magic Orchestra, and played the closing set at Space Lab Yellow in Tokyo, a set that ran for more than 30 hours. He turned 71 in January.

He's still playing those marathon sets, seven and eight hours. He streams often on Twitch, four-hour sessions at a time. He's got a monthly radio show on Worldwide FM. He's writing an autobiography, and he's got a documentary in the works about that New York underground scene.

François: One thing I've observed throughout the arc of a pretty long career is that I tend to pick different things at different times, and not stay focused on the same thing over and over. And that probably accounts for why I always find something that's really exciting, because it always feels kind of fresh.

Simon: One of the ways that curiosity is expressing itself right now is a technique he calls Live Stems. He uses machine learning to pull apart classic recordings, loads the parts into separate players and rebuilds the whole thing live, improvising. This is the technique and the philosophy, in his words.

François: It's very gratifying, because I'm able to use this to bring music that people know, are familiar with, and perform it in a unique and never-again-will-be-heard-in-the-same-way kind of fashion, totally improvised in front of them.

So what it means is that I'm able to create endless variations and new versions of things they've heard forever, in ways that are very endearing, and that kind of bring me back to the beginning of what we were doing manually in the studio 45 years ago, when computers were not part of the equation.

And again, what I'm doing right now, it's all live. It's all done on the fly in front of people, in the moment. And I think there's an incredible value to this.

Simon: Looking back, we asked him next about where that education really began: New York City in the late 1970s, and three clubs that shaped, in many ways, everything that came afterwards, Paradise Garage, The Loft and Better Days. We talked about what it meant to move through those spaces, and what he's carried from them into his work today.

François: Back in that time, not just New York City, but the whole entire world was very different. Today there's a large number of people who equate disco with Boney M. and ABBA and Village People, over-the-top commercial groups that arguably had very, very successful runs of hot disco kind of things. But to us in New York City back in the early 80s, it really was about a type of music that was much more futuristic.

It still blended all the traditional and classic influences of soul music, of Motown, of Stax, of all the great R&B, soul and other types of music that reflected the Black experience. And we were able to congregate in places that those mainstream people I spoke about before would have never been interested in, because it was a different kind of community.

Today these places have gained great significance. They were extremely influential: they influenced major radio stations like WBLS, which was basically one of the top radio stations in America.

They had an oppressive breath of a culture that basically marginalised them, and this is where all of that is born from. And I think part of the reason why it still remains as vital as it does today is because, beyond being the expression of a specific cultural viewpoint, it represented a lifeline for a lot of those who went to these venues.

I think that, to some degree, that is still valid today, especially with the LGBTQ communities. You could argue that this is still the case in many places around the world. So I don't find it that different, to be honest, because I tend to gravitate around those kinds of places today.

Just last weekend, for example, I was in Toronto, where I did a back-to-back six-hour set with Colleen 'Cosmo' Murphy. The next day was Theo Parrish doing a 10-hour set all afternoon, at a venue called Standard Time. And again, it's kind of the same pattern: people who are more on the artistic side of things, more on what we call, loosely, underground, finding places where they feel it's totally great to congregate and be away from the air-quote mainstream, if we could call it. I think that's what it's always been about.

And not to deny that sometimes certain people have had massive hits, like Chic, 'Good Times', or records like that that completely crossed over. But at the beginning, at the core of it, I think dance music and disco was a social phenomenon. And I think it reflected the idea that inclusiveness, diversity and so much more were part of the core values of what we should try to espouse. And sadly, given what we see around the world with certain political movements, I think it's still as relevant as ever.

Sometimes I'll play certain things that might shock people: a harsh drum and bass record right in the middle of a disco set, or a reggae track or dancehall right in the middle of something that was more like house, just because I feel it's needed or necessary.

Or me playing a Killing Joke record in the middle of something that was more electronic. I'd rather you remember those moments, even if you didn't really appreciate them for what they were, instead of leaving the gig not remembering anything because it was all perfectly streamlined, insipid, and only designed for the moment and not for anything else but that.

So that's really a choice, and I think I've kind of cast my fate to the wind with that a long time ago, because I'm kind of known for doing things like this. So are certain other DJs. Certainly, I can think of Laurent Garnier as someone who's kind of known for doing this. But that's the person I am. If I want to play a Hendrix record in the middle of what I'm doing, I will do it.

And sadly, I think that with the pressures of modern life, social media, mass exposure, a lot of DJs have become very, very risk-averse, whether it's because their manager is telling them not to do it, or because they want to get booked again, or this or that, who knows.

But I think, at the core of it, what strikes me as very important is to never forget that connection with people, and that part of what we should be doing is to express thoughts, ideas and artistic concepts that somehow can inspire others, instead of keeping them just sedated.
